speechtext:
1.	Is it true that the inmates in the Kingston penitentiary, of whom 30 per cent are French speaking, cannot benefit from the services of any French speaking teacher?

speechtext:
1.
There are three teachers on the staff of the
Kingston penitentiary, of whom one can converse reasonably well in French, but not to the extent of being able to teach in French. Correspondence courses are available to all inmates in both French and English. The stated percentage of 30 per cent of French speaking inmates needs clarification, inasmuch as this percentage estimate is based on the inmate's family name and not on the language spoken on a day to day basis. ACCEPTANCE OF SANITARY CODE BY RAILWAYS
speechtext: With respect to the Department of National Health and Welfare's national sanitary code applicable to Canadian railways, has this code been accepted and implemented fully by all railroads in Canada and, if not, what parts of the code have not been implemented by what railways?

speakeroldname: Hon. A. J. MacEachen (Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare; Minister of Amateur Sport
subtopic: ACCEPTANCE OF SANITARY CODE BY RAILWAYS
speechtext:
The potable water regulations for common carriers which have been in effect under successive orders in council since 1923 are being implemented without significant difficulties. It is generally recognized that water and ice made available on common carriers for consumption by the public are safe and free from harmful bacteria and chemicals. From time to time, sanitary officers of the Department of National Health and Welfare detect deviations from the practices or equipment specified in the regulations. These are brought to the attention of the railway authorities and corrective action as prescribed by the department is carried out by them.
In 1966 a set of additional standards was developed by the Department of National Health and Welfare after consideration of the views of the Canadian Railway Association and representatives of employee organizations, and recommended for implementation. Implementation is proceeding as older equipment is being replaced by new, or as governed by negotiation between labour and management. It is anticipated that complete implementation will require a considerable time. No detailed inventory of progress is maintained in the Department of National Health and Welfare.

APPLICATION OF EASTERN TIME ZONE TO MARITIME PROVINCES
speechtext: Has any consideration recently been given to the possibility of the maritime provinces of Canada, or some of them, becoming part of the eastern time zone?

speakeroldname: Mr. Jack Davis (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subtopic: APPLICATION OF EASTERN TIME ZONE TO MARITIME PROVINCES
speechtext:
No consideration has been given by the Department of Energy, Mines and Resources to the possibility of the maritime provinces of Canada, or some of them, becoming part of the eastern time zone.
The time service section at the Dominion Observatory, though charged by order in council P.C. 6784 dated August 28, 1941, as the custodian of correct time for official purposes in Canada, has no authority for the definition or regulation of time zone boundaries and there is no federal regulatory body or office in Canada to review and revise time zone boundaries.
Each province has legislation regulating the time being observed within provincial boundaries. From time to time these regulations are modified to accommodate the wish of a community near the zone boundary to adopt the time and the adjacent zone.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise for the purpose of moving the adjournment of the house in accordance with standing order 26 to discuss a matter of urgent public importance, namely the startling disclosures made by the president of the Bank of Western Canada to the effect that:
(a)	the directors of the British International Finance (Canada) Limited and Wellington Financial Corporation Limited, now the York-Lambton Financial Corporation, and/or subsidiary corporations have endeavoured to attempt to get credit from the Bank of Western Canada;
(b)	that the said company or its subsidiaries are engaged in a borrowing operation with
Bank of Western Canada United States banks which involves the giving of an option of 10 per cent of the total shares of the Bank of Western Canada and various arrangements designed to tie the management and operations of the bank to the operations of these United States banks, again contrary to statements made when applying for a charter, which disclosures indicate that the applicants for charter for the said bank, in making their presentation to the committee of the House of Commons on finance, trade and economic affairs, misled the committee and the House of Commons, in contempt of parliament.
I move that motion, Mr. Speaker, seconded by the hon. member for Perth (Mr. Monteith).

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: BANK OF WESTERN CANADA-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: Would the Leader of the Opposition address the Chair on the question of urgency of debate at this time.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: BANK OF WESTERN CANADA-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am not going into the detail of the allegations made over the week end by the president of the Bank of Western Canada, except to say that his allegations charged that the intent of the legislation granting a charter to the bank, with the express proviso of the Treasury Board granting exemption from certain clauses of the legislation, has been infringed by the controlling organization, British International Finance, in a way to countermand the wishes and intent of parliament.
When the rights and privileges of parliament have been contravened and a prima facie case has been made out, no other matter can take primacy in this House of Commons. In other words the rights and privileges of parliament cannot be shamelessly treated or contemptuously disregarded. Whenever that takes place the urgency thereof is second to no other field or area of legislative responsibility in parliament.
It might be said that the budget debate will be commencing soon and that therefore this matter can be discussed at that time. It is difficult enough to get answers in parliament at any time during debate; how much more difficult in a matter such as this. I would hope the government would immediately agree to the adjournment of the house, to the end that the basic foundations upon which our financial institutions stand, namely integrity and honesty in the presentation of grounds for incorporation, are in no way undermined.
This is a specific issue, Mr. Speaker, dealing with the conditions under which a charter was granted by parliament and expanded by Treasury Board in its decision to exempt this
12676	COMMONS
Bank of Western Canada particular bank from the provisions forbidding concentration of ownership in a proportion greater than 10 per cent. The exemption was granted, one of the conditions being that there would not be financial intercourse between the Bank of Western Canada and the controlling companies with the bank being in the position of a lender. According to the president of the Bank of Western Canada this provision, by a species of financial wizardry, has been swept aside and abrogated.
[DOT] (2:50 p.m.)
Indeed, what can be more urgent than the president's statement to the effect that there had been an attempt to breach the conditions set down by Treasury Board, in other words a deliberate, intentional and indeed planned flouting of undertakings given again and again to parliament in the committee-and I have the various quotations here-to the effect that the Bank of Western Canada would not under any circumstances become a kind of milch cow for the Stevens group. Yet that is one of the things the president says is being attempted.
If the facts alleged by the president of the bank are true we have an issue that goes to the heart of parliament's rights. Parliament must go into the financial operations of this group, the Stevens group from Toronto, and British International Finance Corporation. It must look into the power that has been accumulated over six years when less than $300,000 of capital, by reason of interlocking directorates and other manipulations, has given two or three men control over $130 million of capital in various corporations, the Wellington Bank, York-Lambton Financial Corporation, York Trust, Canada First Mortgage, and so on.
These are matters that cannot be dealt with in a budget debate. We cannot get answers. I was away for a few days during the recent debate on unification. On reading the reports I find I missed nothing in the way of information. The minister gave no information at all.
We want to guard against that. We ask for the opportunity of debate, to learn whether the allegations are correct and to put an end to the kind of financial operation exemplified by Mr. Stevens saying that the president of the Bank of Western Canada had only a $7,600 interest in these corporations. What business had Mr. Stevens to say that? That type of arrogance deserves to be looked into. Parliament has the right to investigate this matter. Every hour of delay leaves open the
[Mr. Diefenbaker.l
DEBATES	February 6, 1967
door for further important financial repercussions which affect the lives of Canadians. We do not want another financial mess on our hands such as we have had recently.
There has been too much nonchalance regarding these financial matters. I say they must be dealt with now. They require the fullest inquiry. We want to know from the government whether there was deception.
I have here the record of the evidence given in the committee. I say, on the basis of the evidence given by Mr. Stevens, what has taken place here is a flouting of the pledged word. The whole labyrinthine complex of the Stevens combine must be looked into. It cannot be done by questions. Questions have been asked all the way through. On December 1, 15 and 16 I endeavoured to secure from the minister or Prime Minister some indication of concern by this government regarding what was being done. On January 17 I again raised the matter with regard to the Treasury Board exemption. On January 18 the Minister of Finance tabled Treasury Board Order No. 658,534. The hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands asked what was the meaning of the series of operations reported in the press, in December, having the effect of concentrating control in the hands of a few individuals. The minister promised to look into it, but a licence to operate was issued regardless.
This is a serious matter, something which cannot be glossed over. This is the first opportunity parliament has had to inquire into it. There is no other way in which we, on behalf of the Canadian people, can ensure that such experiences as Prudential Finance, insurance company bankruptcies and the like shall not become permanent features of the financial landscape. Nothing comes before the right of members of parliament to examine and crossexamine. They received an assurance that these things would not take place. Now the president of the bank resigns because he says that undertakings honestly given, as he says, have been contravened. We cannot shut our eyes to the revelations which have been made.

subtopic: BANK OF WESTERN CANADA-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
As Your Honour is aware, I had prepared a motion to the same effect as that prepared by the Leader of the Opposition, though I must say at the outset that I had hoped a statement from the Minister of Finance would have obviated the necessity for presenting such motions. Indeed, I am
February 6, 1967	COMMONS
somewhat surprised that he did not seize the opportunity when it arose.
As to the matter of urgency of debate, I think really there can be no question about that. Here we have a situation in which, for the first time in many, many years, a chartered bank of Canada-and no matter how slightly the Bank of Western Canada has entered into the banking field it is now one of Canada's chartered banks-comes under the winds of suspicion. I suggest that unless the government is prepared to announce certain action to correct the situtation we may well create a lack of confidence in the whole banking structure, something which we in this country cannot afford.
Another argument in respect of urgency is that at this very moment we are in the process of carrying out the decennial revision of the Bank Act, which is now before the committee on finance and economic affairs. If something is to be done about this specific case something must also be done about the arrangements which were made under the Bank Act and certain provisions in the bill before us. I do not think this is a matter which can be left where it is in the absence of a declaration by the government of Canada clearly indicating that this is an occasion for serious concern, especially when it arises, as it does, after a number of events in the financial world which have badly shaken the confidence of the Canadian people. Also, I might say, the government's reluctance to assert its authority in some areas in which it is suggested there is no doubt about its provenance gives rise to a certain amount of misgiving and apprehension as to whether the government is fully seized of the nature of the events now revealed by the president of the Bank of Western Canada.
Before I close, may I say I think we should commend Mr. Coyne for his frankness in bringing this matter before the people of Canada. He may have been naive in his choice of business associates, but I suggest no member of this house and no member of the public has ever had any doubts about Mr. Coyne's honesty and integrity. I urge you to accept this motion, Mr. Speaker, so the people of Canada may be reassured with regard to the affairs of one of the chartered banks of Canada.

With regard to the importance of the topic which has been raised at this time, in my opinion there can be no doubt that a trust has been violated so far as this house is concerned, and to have something like this come up at a time when we are considering the over-all banking picture is certainly very disturbing. I believe it is in the national interest that it be dealt with as quickly as possible.
I join with the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands in saying that one would have thought the Minister of Finance would have taken the lead and made a statement on motions, because it was only to be expected that this important matter would be raised today.
Notwithstanding the fact that the committee on finance, trade and economic affairs is currently meeting and the Minister of Finance is appearing before it as a witness, I believe the importance of this issue is such that it is imperative we debate it. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think it is highly desirable that the charges made by Mr. Coyne should be investigated, but I doubt very much whether they can be successfully investigated on a motion to adjourn the house.
Mr. Coyne has made certain specific charges against his colleagues in the Bank of Western Canada. I believe those should be investigated. This morning I also received a message from Mr. Sinclair Stevens which I should like to read:
I am sorry I missed speaking with you at the Park Plaza yesterday and I was unable to contact you by telephone this morning but I wish to assure you that my associates and myself are more than willing to meet with you personally or to appear before any committee or other group that you may feel desirable to clarify or contradict statements which are attributed to Mr. Coyne in the press.
Sinclair Stevens.
I do believe it is highly desirable, Mr. Speaker, that both Mr. Coyne and Mr. Stevens should appear before the committee
February 6, 1967

Bank of Western Canada of this house on finance, trade and economic affairs, before which the original application for the charter of the Bank of Western Canada was heard and where Mr. Coyne, incidentally, would like to make some suggestions about further amendments to the Bank Act.
Personally I have no difficulty in dealing with the government's responsibility in this matter, but before I am asked to make a judgment, which I am required to make under the act, I would like to know what the issues are, and I do believe that we would better advance the business of the house and the business of the nation, in which we are all interested, if these charges and the reply of Mr. Stevens could be heard before the standing committee of the house which is charged at the moment with the amendments to the Bank Act.
Moreover, Mr. Speaker, if we just wanted to have a general discussion about this matter, there is ample scope in the budget debate.

subtopic: BANK OF WESTERN CANADA-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I say a word on the matter of urgency. The Minister of Finance has argued that this matter should be investigated but that it can be more properly investigated by the standing committee on finance, trade and economic affairs, and that he would be quite prepared to make a statement to the house but it is necessary that he know what the charges are.
I want to suggest to Your Honour that the matter of urgency has not to do solely with the question of charges by Mr. Coyne. The matter of urgency has to do with the manner in which the Minister of Finance himself has been discharging his responsibilities. The commitments which were made by the Bank of Western Canada through the banking committee of the House of Commons prior to the bank's incorporation are one thing, but there is an agreement between the Treasury Board and the Bank of Western Canada, which arose out of the extension of the ownership clause to allow them to hold more than 50 per cent of the stock. That agreement was specific in setting out what the bank could not do. It could not make loans to the B.I.F. companies; it could not deposit money with those companies, that it could not guarantee any liability of that financial group or purchase any assets from that financial complex.
It seems to me the house has a right to a statement from the minister as to whether this agreement has been complied with,

whether any of the provisions of this agreement have been violated or circumvented. It is not now a matter of the charges of Mr. Coyne versus Mr. Sinclair Stevens. The question at the moment is whether the Minister of Finance, who is the watchdog for parliament and the Canadian people with respect to the operations of this bank, has been doing his duty, and whether he can assure this parliament that the bank has complied fully with the agreement.
If he cannot tell us that, then we are in a bad way. If there has been no investigation, or if there has been no supervision, then certainly we are in a bad way. Surely we do not have to depend on Mr. Coyne and Mr. Stevens to tell the house whether an agreement, entered into between a chartered bank and the Canadian Treasury Board, has been lived up to in every detail. It seems to me this is a matter which makes it most urgent that the subject be discussed.
There is also the matter of the bank itself to be considered, and public confidence in it. This will not be cleared up until the Minister of Finance has given us the kind of assurance that I have suggested he ought to be able to give us at this time.

I refer hon. members to citation 100(3) in Beauchesne's fourth edition:
"Urgency" within this rule does not apply to the matter itself, but it means "urgency of debate", when the ordinary opportunities provided by the rules of the house do not permit the subject to be brought on early enough and public interest demands that discussion take place immediately.
I am in full agreement with the submissions made by the right hon. Leader of the Opposition, the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands and the other hon.
February 6, 1967	COMMONS
members that this is a matter of urgency, but the house is in a position where, within an hour or so, we will revert to consideration of the budget.
A suggestion was made by the Leader of the Opposition that it might be easier for the opposition to obtain information and the views of the government if the debate on this important matter were held under the terms of standing order 26 rather than in the course of the discussion on the budget, but I cannot agree with this suggestion. It seems to me that the only difference between one debate and the other is that speeches during the budget debate are limited to 30 minutes, and speeches in a debate under standing order 26 could be for 40 minutes. That is the only procedural distinction I can see between the two types of debate.
Hon. members will have an opportunity to make their statements later on this afternoon and in the course of the evening, and for all intents and purposes I would think we would achieve the same objectives during the budget debate as those which are sought at the present time by the mover of the motion, the right hon. Leader of the Opposition.

speakerposition: subtopic
subtopic: THE BUDGET

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: The house resumed, from Monday, December 19, consideration of the motion of Hon. Mitchell Sharp (Minister of Finance) that Mr. Speaker do now leave the chair for the house to go into committee of ways and means, and the amendment thereto of Mr. Monteith.

subtopic: THE BUDGET
subsubtopic: ADDITIONAL FINANCIAL MEASURES OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in resuming the budget debate which was adjourned some time ago I want to say that it is very difficult to say anything about the budget because in my opinion and that of my colleagues it was an entirely unnecessary exercise in which the Minister of Finance indulged last December. I think it was shameful of him to have attempted it, and I suggest it was a deliberate attempt on his part to frighten the Canadian people away from seeking increases in social welfare programs from now on with the threat that there would be an immediate and equivalent increase in taxes.
[DOT] (3:40 p.m.)
This becomes clear, Mr. Speaker, when we look at some of the statements which he made
The Budget-Mr. Lewis on December 19 when he introduced this so-called mini-budget. He said that he was introducing these taxes because it was necessary for the people of Canada to realize that every time they want any social expenditures, taxes for them must be found. At page 11332 of Hansard the minister is recorded as saying:
It is because we are in that position that tonight we are asking the Canadian public to accept increased taxes in order that we may distribute more to our old age pensioners with low incomes.
This was an inaccurate statement, Mr. Speaker. It was a deliberately misleading statement to the Canadian people. The minister had the funds and admitted that he had the funds to distribute more to our old age pensioners on low incomes. He admitted he had the funds until at least this coming spring when he would bring down the regular budget. I suggest his statement was a deliberate misrepresentation of the financial position.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: THE BUDGET
subsubtopic: ADDITIONAL FINANCIAL MEASURES OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Order. I am sure, knowing the hon. member for York South, he would not want to use words which are obviously unparliamentary. No hon. member can say in the House of Commons of Canada that a statement made by another hon. member is deliberately misleading.

subtopic: THE BUDGET
subsubtopic: ADDITIONAL FINANCIAL MEASURES OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I am sorry, Mr. Speaker; I will put it this way without casting the aspersion which my previous words contained. The effect of the statement was to give a false picture of the financial position of the old age security fund in that the minister's own tables showed there was enough money in it to take care of the old age pensioners under the supplementary payments bill without requiring further taxation. In fact, time and time again in his speech the minister seemed to me to be waving his admonitory forefinger at the people of Canada as if they were school children and telling them that if they ever wanted any more social welfare they must remember they would have to pay for it and pay for it immediately no matter what the circumstances may be.
There was no reason for the budget, Mr. Speaker. Indeed, the Minister of Finance said two things about the Canadian economy during his speech on December 19 which clearly emphasized the fact there was no reason for the budget. After reviewing the situation and the developments in the past three months, the minister is recorded as saying at page 11332 of Hansard:
Developments in the past three months, however, suggest to me that the undesirable acceleration of the demands upon our economy has moderated. There has been some economic readjustment taking

February 6, 1967
The Budget-Mr. Lewis place following the excessive rates of expansion that occurred earlier this year. The effects of a large number of strikes have also been appearing in the statistics. My judgment is that the economic expansion now taking place is more in line with the capability of our economy to grow steadily without inflation.
This was a clear statement that there was nothing in the development of the economy at that time that justified any action by him in withdrawing any part of the purchasing power of the Canadian people. Later in his speech he certainly emphasized two or three times that in December the economic situation could not be foretold, that he had to wait, if I remember correctly, for the situation to become clearer in the United States, that events were still in a state of development and it was impossible for him to make any definitive forecast about the economy in 1967.
What does that add up to, Mr. Speaker, except a statement to the house and to the country that in fact he did not have the information necesssary to take any fiscal measures which would be related to the economic requirements of Canada? This is what he said. So far as he was able to see, the economy had levelled off, economic expansion had slowed down and no action by him was necessary. I suggest to him that he was going around the mulberry bush. At one point he said we needed no action, at another point he said he was not in a position to take action, and at a third point he said he was taking "neutral action".
What does neutral action mean? As I listened to him and as I reread his speech, I wondered what he meant. It reminded me of some people who talk about equality and insist that some people are more equal than others. It seemed to me that his December budget was a little more neutral than others. It was intended to have no effect, but it is having a deleterious effect on the economy and particularly one part of it to which I shall refer in a moment.
I really listened to the minister with amazement and I read his speech with even greater amazement. It is clearly obvious that there were only two reasons for introducing the budget. The first one was that in September, perhaps out of genuine fear of what he called inflationary pressures, he undertook to introduce a mini-budget. When December came he found it really was not necessary, but he felt that he was committed to take an unnecessary and unwise step. The second reason I have already given. It seems to me the minister was deliberately setting out to slow

down social progress in Canada, to warn the Canadian people that from now on, so far as he and his colleagues are concerned, the progress of the Canadian people in regard to welfare would have to be slowed down because he said that we can no longer afford these vast payments. I say, Mr. Speaker, that this is a retrograde step, a regressive policy, an unjustified attitude in these modern times. He and I hope, as does everyone in Canada, that the Canadian economy will continue to expand. I say to him that it will be as unnecessary in the future as it has been unnecessary in the past to match welfare increases by precise increases in taxes. This is what his budget did.
I always hate even trying to be technical about these things, but it seems to me the budget was extremely illogical in another way. If the minister had come before parliament last spring and given an indication he intended to come before parliament this spring with the proposition that he must balance his budget in every way, then I could understand him attempting to balance the particular expenditures under the old age supplementary payments bill. I would not agree with him but I could understand it. However, in the same speech in which he insists he must increase taxes to raise precisely the amount it will cost to implement old age supplementary assistance payments, he also tells us the budgetary deficit is going to be greater than the amount he estimated last spring. This action, I suggest, emphasizes and underlines my suspicion that he sought to place the situation before the people of Canada in such a way as to make certain that from now on Canadians will be frightened to ask for improvement in the welfare of the young, the old or the ill because immediately they will be faced with an equal adjustment in their taxes.
[DOT] (3:50 p.m.)
I feel that this action is both unreasonable and undesirable. However, if the minister came to the conclusion that he needed a tax increase, we in this party, think that one half of the steps he took was correct. We disagree that there was any need at all for a tax increase, for the reasons I have tried to indicate. But if the minister determined that he was going to increase taxes he was certainly right in increasing the special income tax which is related to the old age security fund. As far as we are concerned the minister should have raised the ceiling even higher
February G, 1967

than he did if he wanted more money than this increase will provide.
A careful study of the minister's budget speech shows the following situation, which really condemns beyond words his increase in the sales tax. At page 11335 of Hansard appears Table 2 of his budget speech and, basing himself upon the table, the minister said, as reported in the first paragraph on page 11336.
It will be seen that with this increased maximum tax-
The increased maximum tax related to the old age security fund.

the requirements of the fund, to which the law directs our attention, are met until the end of the 1970-71 fiscal year, the first full year after the age reduction program is complete.
What reason then is there, Mr. Speaker, for any further tax? If, as the table at page 11335 of Hansard shows, the increase in income tax in connection with the old age security fund will place the fund in such a position that it will have the necessary money to meet the progressive reduction in the age of recipients as well as the additional payments under the old age supplementary payments bill for the next five years until 1970-71 what possible reason or justification can there be for an increase in another tax?
According to the minister's argument, which I reject, it was necessary for him to raise the additional funds by way of tax. Enough money was raised for five years by the simple increase of the maximum rate of the old age security tax from $120 to $240 a year. That, Mr. Speaker, gave him all he wanted from now till the first year the full program of age reduction is complete, sufficient. I repeat, not only for the $75 a month old age security pension but also, as the table clearly shows, for the additional payments that will have to be made under the supplementary payments legislation.
Despite the fact he had already raised sufficient money-which I repeat he did not have to do in the first place-to meet his requirements, the minister then imposed a totally injustified additional 1 per cent on the sales tax. I must say he did it with some obvious feeling of shame and regret. He himself admitted that it was a regressive tax and almost apologized for imposing it. Nonetheless he did so while at the same time making more exemptions, exceptions and long apologies.
I have tried to understand why the minister took this step, and again I can only repeat my earlier suggestion, that it is his determination
The Budget-Mr. Lewis to rap the knuckles of the Canadian people for wanting any advance in the welfare services or of the people in Canada who require welfare assistance of any sort. If I may summarize, there was no reason for any budget at all. But if there was any reason whatever for raising extra revenue this was fully accomplished by the progressive increase in the income tax and there was no justification for any additional increase in the sales tax.
As reported at page 11337 the minister said:
The increase in sales tax can be expected to increase the prices of those goods subject to it-
I stop in the middle of a sentence. Here is a gentleman who for a year has been crying about what he called inflationary pressures in the economy. This is a government that has been faced with constant increases in the cost of living. We have a situation in Canada where the housewives of this country have been protesting against increases in prices. A joint committee has been dealing with the problem of the rising cost of living. Without any necessity whatever for his action, and after he has met all his requirements, the minister puts on the statute books an increase in the sales tax and blandly says that the increase in sales tax can be expected to increase the prices of those goods that are subject to it.
I am aware, of course, that food and some other things are excluded from sales tax, but this sales tax hits the housewife in many other areas: clothing, fixtures, household appliances, furniture and all the other things a family needs. To impose an additional 1 per cent at a time when it is totally unnecessary and the economy does not require it is an act of sheer thoughtlessness for which the only explanation, as I have said, is the desire of the minister to rap the knuckles of the Canadian people.
The fact of the matter is that despite his action of not putting the additional 1 per cent on certain building materials, this increase has already had an effect on prices. In the same paragraph from which I have already quoted-I am not going to take the time to re-quote it, but if you will permit me to paraphrase it the minister can correct me if I paraphrase it wrongly-the minister said that in his opinion the increase should be very minimal; it should be less than 1 per cent, he said.
The fact is that there have already been price increases announced in the press of 2 per cent, li per cent and more than 2 per cent on many of the goods on which this sales

February 6. 1967
The Budget-Mr. Lewis tax falls, as could have been foretold by him and his advisers. There are situations where an increase of 1 per cent on a certain item would be so small a fraction of a cent that the manufacturers or others would take advantage of the 1 per cent increase in sales tax to get to the nearest half cent or full cent increase in prices, with the result that the total increase is, in fact, 2 per cent or more. Once more I ask the Minister of Finance what possible justification he can have for this thoughtless addition to the cost of living in Canada today.
I have in my hands a letter which one of my colleagues received from a building materials firm, and one paragraph reads as follows:
Prior to the current increase-
That is, prior to the current increase in the sales tax.
-it was possible to make up a bid using 11 per cent on everything. Now it is necessary to take some items at 11 per cent and the increased items at 12 per cent. This causes no end of work to all the trade and will no doubt result in considerable extra expense for the department, as it will entail a far greater amount of checking into the various accounts.
I have the suspicion, Mr. Speaker, that if a mistake occurs it will likely be on the side of 12 per cent than on the side of 11 per cent.
In my view, the minister ought to have looked in particular at the effect of this tax increase on housing. Instead of increasing the sales tax by 1 per cent, he should have given careful consideration to the housing needs of this country and to the question whether it was not his duty to remove the sales tax on housing materials and building supplies entirely. I suggest to him that that was his duty. It was not his duty to increase the sales tax by 1 per cent.
[DOT] (4:00 p.m.)
We are faced in this country, as the minister and every member knows, with a serious housing crisis. Everybody uses the term. In this country, in parliaments and legislatures, we have got into the habit of dealing in percentages and global figures-millions, hundreds of millions and billions of dollars. We talk of houses in terms of large numbers of homes. Sometimes I feel, when we use these figures, particularly when they are large figures, that we forget we are really speaking of the plight of thousands of Canadian families, men, women, and particularly children, who have to live in unsanitary homes, unpleasant surroundings leading to broken

homes and juvenile delinquency. That is what we speak of when we talk of housing figures. Those figures represent broken lives in Canada. The Minister of Finance had a moral and social duty to be concerned about the broken lives of people living in unsanitary homes. He ought not to be concerned with the silly promise he made last September which he felt obliged to implement in December despite changing economic circumstances.
The housing facts have been placed on the record time and time again. Until this government acts and until some of the provincial governments join with it to take adequate action. They will have to be repeated. In 1965 housing starts in Toronto, in round figures, totalled 30,000; in 1966 they were about 21,000, a decrease of 30 per cent. According to the authorities we need at least 40,000 new homes in Toronto-I have been dealing with Toronto and my figures were for that city alone. Instead of 40,000 new dwellings started in 1966, 21,000 were started, about 50 per cent of the requirements of that metropolitan area.
In the whole of Canada there are about
50.000	publicly owned low rental housing units, less than 1 per cent of all dwellings in the country. The 1961 census showed that
923.000	households, just short of 1 million, in this country lived in broken down, crowded or unsanitary homes. The likelihood now is that instead of the number being under one million it has risen to about one and a half million. A great many Canadians are living in such homes.
In Vancouver from 400 to 500 families are on the waiting list for public housing, and less than half the required number of units are scheduled for completion within the next two years. They are not even completed now. This sort of thing is true right across the country. In every urban area the housing lack is disastrous for the people of Canada.
1 do not refer only to new homes. Slum areas ought to be redeveloped. There is a lack of parks and recreational facilities. Air and water are polluted. All these factors are making life for many hundreds of thousands of Canadians in our larger metropolitan areas really unpleasant, unsanitary and uncomfortable.
This is the situation the minister ought to have dealt with last December and for which he ought to have made provision so that the Minister of Labour responsible for housing might have made in this house a statement that really meant something when dealing with the housing crisis. Instead, we had the
February 6, 1967

picayune policy announcement which my leader justifiably and graphically described as giving a peanut to an elephant to assuage his hunger. Because the minister and the government fail to deal with the basic issues facing the Canadian people we get little bits here and little bits there, slowly, totally inadequately, and totally undesirable in most instances.
Since the minister was determined to make a budget speech in December-I suggest he could have spared himself the trouble and us the pain had he looked at the economy and the situation then-he should also have been concerned, as he says he is, with a matter about which his colleague, the Minister without Portfolio from Toronto, is so terribly concerned. I assume that the question of the lack of adequate control by Canada of its own industry and resources must be of great concern to the present Minister of Finance. Unlike another minister of the government, he agreed to serve on the special committee of ministers going into this question. I suggest to hon. members, and this is without disrespect for the Minister without Portfolio from Toronto for whom I have a great regard, that in parliamentary history there probably is no parallel for a member of parliament being invited to rejoin the cabinet and then being promptly appointed chairman of a royal commission of inquiry. This is what the committee of ministers to look into these matters is really about.
I say to the Minister of Finance and to the government that the New Democratic Party and others have waited for years for the long promised Canadian Development Corporation. At its founding convention in 1961 our party suggested that one of the best ways of regaining greater control over Canada's economy was to establish a publicly organized, publicly directed and managed-I emphasize totally publicly directed and managed-Canadian development fund, as we called it. In it would be gathered the savings of the Canadian people in appropriate ways. In it would be placed such savings as insurance companies and the like hold, voluntarily if possible but by a requirement of the law if necessary. Such a Canadian development fund would then have the necessary savings of Canadians to invest in new industries, in underdeveloped regions of this country and, whenever necessary, in repatriating parts of the economy it may be desirable to repatriate. Two or three years after 1961 we heard from the government that it proposed to establish what it called the
The Budget-Mr. Lewis Canadian Development Corporation. But we find that it is now on the shelf, as are so many things this government has placed there, resting peacefully and gathering dust.
[DOT] (4:10 p.m.)
I suggest to the Minister of Finance and to the house that the concern felt by the people some years ago about Canada's economic selfreliance, Canada's economic independence, ought to be a great deal deeper today than it was even then. The fact is that the control of Canada's economy by foreign corporations continues apace. The reinvestment of undistributed profits by subsidiaries of United States corporations gives them an ever-increasing weight in the economy. Moreover, in the last two or three years there have been examples of interference with the laws and policies of Canada and attempted interference with lines of economic development in this country. All this makes it more important than ever before that we should take steps to give Canada greater economic self-reliance.
I need not recall the famous guide lines which were issued from the United States according to which Canadian subsidiaries of Unites States corporations were required to send their undistributed earnings back home to their parent companies. More recently, if we had any sense of Canadian identity and Canadian pride we all stood aghast at the temerity of the United States authorities in sending sharp notes to the Canadian government with regard to the Mercantile Bank.
Why is not the Canada Development Corporation legislation before us? What is the reason, other than the division in the ranks of the government, the difference of opinion which has been disclosed from time to time between the Minister without Portfolio (Mr. Gordon) and some of his supporters in the cabinet and other ministers with their supporters? The result of this indecision, of this conflict within the ranks of the government, is that an important piece of legislation, one which alone, in our view, can effectively bring about the control of our economy by Canadians, lies on the shelf.
These are the matters with which the minister ought to have been concerned, in my view, last December. I summarize by saying that in my opinion the supplementary budget was unnecessary and the increase in the sales tax was a shameful, undesirable imposition on the people of Canada.

Certainly there is an indication that there is a let-up and I hope this be helpful to our area of Canada in the near future.
I have learned through talking to businessmen that inventories are growing, the number of projects being undertaken has lessened materially, the number of firms looking for the orders has increased greatly and competition is very keen to get what available business there is. As a result lay-offs are occurring in plants which have not had to lay off anyone for a period of five to ten years. If something is not done in the very near future we will be in a lot of trouble and most of it will be related to the tight money policy imposed by the government.
In this regard I should like to say something about housing, because even in a small town like the one in which I live, which has a population of only 11,000 or 12,000 people, there is a very great need for housing. With the amount of interest which has to be paid on the loans necessary in order to build houses today, houses are so far out of the reach of the ordinary person who needs a home that it is impossible for him to assume the obligation that the government today requires.
In addition, the tight money policy of the government always strikes the construction industry and housing first, and the first victim generally speaking is the Canadian who is in the $5,000 to $6,000 income bracket or below. These are the people who really need housing more than anyone else. Yet they are the people who are struck first by the tight money policy. They are the people who find that their hope of owning a home of their own goes out the window completely. I believe that housing in particular should be divorced from the construction industry in so far as government policy is concerned and certainly in so far as its tight-money policy is concerned. But that has not been the case in respect of this government. This is indicated quite significantly by the number of housing starts in recent months. The government has tried to take some meek steps to correct the situation. I like the analogy that was drawn by the leader of the New Democratic Party when he said it was like throwing a peanut to an elephant.

I believe that the government must wake up to this fact. It must come forward with far more constructive housing policies than has been the case to date. Unless this is done, the government will be doing a great disservice to many hard working Canadians who have a right to expect to be able to look forward to owning their own homes but who today do not have a chance in the world of accomplishing this aim.
I should like also to say something about the amendment moved by the hon. member for Perth (Mr. Monteith) in so far as old age security is concerned. Certainly, as was stated by the previous speaker, the funds are available today in the old age security fund. They were there when the increase was approved. They could have been used. Had they been used it would not have been necessary to increase the income tax, but instead the government went forward and in effect gave the taxpayers a spanking for thinking that a $30 increase could be provided even to the needy without someone paying the bill. They said that everybody is going to pay the bill and that this will prove to everybody that they cannot come and ask for money unless they are willing to shell out money.
The funds in the old age security fund were put there by the taxpayers of this nation and they should not be expected to have to pay additional income tax while their own money is sitting in the fund and it is available for the payment of the additional $30 a month to those who can qualify for it. I also think that if the government wishes to talk about a guaranteed annual income and suggest to the Canadian people that the minimum amount which should be available to anyone in this nation is $1,260 per year, then the least it can do is increase the income tax exemption to that amount. In my opinion it is rather ridiculous for the federal government to say we should provide the Canadian people with a guaranteed annual income of $1,260 and then ask these same people to pay income tax on $260 because there is an exemption of only $1,000. Surely to goodness the government cannot talk out of both sides of its mouth at the same time. We should have one thing or the other. We should have a guaranteed annual income, if this is what the government wants, of $1,000 a year-I do not think that would be at all adequate; indeed, I do not think $1,260 is adequate today-or the exemption should be raised so that those people receiving the guaranteed annual income would not have to turn around and give back

Mr. Speaker, I was rather surprised at the turn of the debate this afternoon, having anticipated that in the first round we would hear representations from the minor parties in the house. It is because of an obvious miscalculation in schedules that involved Your Honour as well as other hon. members of the house that possibly there has been a slight shuffling around. It may be that the attitude of the minor parties is a reflection of how important they consider this mini-budget. Frankly, I share their implied attitude.
With the greatest respect to the minister, I think he found himself facing the necessity of bringing in a budget, which he postponed and postponed and finally could not postpone any longer than December 19 if the house was to adjourn on December 21. Therefore there was a fulfilment of the undertaking given by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Sharp) and I think by the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) on a number of occasions in the late summer and early fall, that because of pressing problems concerned with rapidly increasing inflation there would be a budget by Christmas. As a matter of fact, the indication was that there would be a budget well before December 1, as though the presentation of a budget in this house would be a cure-all for any and every economic ill that beset the nation.
I remember that in 1962 there was a great cry by editorial writers and other people who were not favourable to the government, that all that was required in the fall of that year following upon the convertibility crisis of May, 1962, was a budget. Our late colleague, the former hon. member for Digby-Annapolis-Kings, then minister of finance, repeatedly had the taunt thrown at him by government members, then in the official opposition, and other opposition members that never in his career had he presented a budget. When we came back into office after the election in 1962, the election having followed a full budget presention by the then minister of finance, Hon. Donald Fleming, the whole budget was there for everyone to examine. The proposals of the government were before the house and the country.
February 6, 1967

The Budget-Mr. Lambert
It is true that that budget was not debated in the house. But if we understand the nature of a budget debate we know that the proposals of the government are in the main ignored and hon. members discuss subjects which they were not able to discuss during the debate on the speech from the throne. The budget debate settles nothing. It provides a forum for ideas and proposals. That is what this house does. But somehow or other the idea is abroad in the minds of far too many people that the mere fact of presenting a budget, whether it tinkers up or tinkers down, will have salutary effects. In many instances, as is the case with this budget, it matters not a tinker's damn. That is the effect of this budget.
[DOT] (4:50 p.m.)
Frankly speaking, this budget did nothing and it was uncalled for in the light of the circumstances. It was only mooted last summer as a sort of ultimate escape hatch for the government when it failed to deal effectively with certain problems of inflation. The dilemma which faced the Minister of Finance in December was whether or not he should tax, whether or not he should apply a damper or whether he should leave the situation pretty well as it is. The dilemma he faced was one which was perplexing economic experts not only in Canada but in the United States. This is an indication of the close affiliation between the two economies, the United States economy being the dominant one and ours not being an exact mirror of theirs but following its movements in so far as United States interest rates are concerned.
We have heard cries about tight money as though this was only a Canadian phenomenon. However, the truth of the matter is that restrictions on credit appeared in the United States before they did here. The United States has experienced additional pressure on credit facilities primarily because of the demands of the war effort in connection with the conflict in Viet Nam and also the demands of the space program. We in Canada have not had such pressures to the same extent. There was inflation in the United States similar to that in Canada. There have been price hikes in basic commodities in the United States, such as we have had, and they have been controlled in some cases by executive action in that country. We in Canada saw the same sort of action taken with regard to a certain increase in the cost of steel which was announced by a number of companies in the late summer.

The government is becoming very much aware of the fact that the Canadian people themselves are not providing the necessary investment funds for the development of our industry and the control of our industry.
Why is this so? It is because they do not have the money left to invest. More and more funds are being channelled into the public sector, not for the development or control of industry and our resources but for public expenditures such as transfer payments. We must come to a decision as to what we are going to do. Are we going to take away the funds that could be in large measure devoted to the purchase of equities for the development and production of Canadian resources which in the end would guarantee the basic economic strength necessary for Canadians to look after themselves?
In my view there must come a point where the individual still has the responsibility, still has the right to make up his mind, but this is being denied to him. Every program that comes along is compulsory and is framed in the so-called language of universality. If the individual is to make up his mind as to how he will provide for his old age, by investment in this or that pension plan, surely this process will provide funds for investment in the private sector. We know that this year $600 million was taken out of the economy compulsorily for the Canada Pension Plan. I am not saying all that would have been destined for investment in the private sector but certainly a great proportion of it would have been. However, it has been withdrawn and turned over to the provincial governments who in turn may hand some of it over to the municipalities for spending on various undertakings, many of which would require a second look as to timing. When it comes to having money available for investment, say in the tar sands, and one requires $250 million one finds that the private sector of the Canadian economy does not have that kind of money.
There are many other areas in which I feel the Canadian public should be encouraged to invest in the Canadian economy. There was a certain approach when the hon. member for Davenport (Mr. Gordon) was minister of finance, and there are still regrettable vestiges of this policy prevalent in government

I feel there is a great deal more merit in encouraging Canadians to invest rather than in discouraging foreigners from investing in Canada. I feel that a positive program of incentives is not going to cost that much money and in the end there will be an increase in the economic development of Canada by Canadians.
In the over-all picture of government budgeting it matters not whether certain moneys have to be spent in a certain way or whether less money comes in by another means. Mr. Speaker, I find it very interesting to note that less than three hours ago we were involved in a debate on the setting aside of the normal business of the house in order to debate the urgent problem that had arisen in regard to the Bank of Western Canada and the resignation of the president of that bank from several financial corporations in Toronto with which he had previously been connected. At that time, Mr. Speaker, your advice in disallowing the plea for urgency was that the matter could be raised in the budget debate which was to follow. We are now embarked upon that debate and have been so engaged for several hours. The afternoon is well advanced but we have yet to hear any mention of the subject which would have set aside the normal business of the house.
It is not my intention, Mr. Speaker, to dwell on that matter at any length now, though this does not detract from the importance and urgency of dealing with it. I found some of the remarks the Minister of Finance (Mr. Sharp) made in regard to the matter most interesting, particularly the reference to his telephone conversation with Mr. Stevens. As the hon. gentleman will be before the committee tonight I am sure we will hear further remarks from him at that time. I trust that both Mr. Stevens and Mr. Coyne will be brought before the committee on finance and economic affairs at the very earliest opportunity so that we can hear directly from those two gentlemen.
Certainly if the Bank of Western Canada is to be a bank the operations of which are particularly aimed at serving the interests and needs of western Canadians, then the stand that Mr. Coyne is taking is a most 23033-803i
The Budget-Mr. Thompson commendable one. Whether the bank is controlled from Bay street or whether it is controlled from Wall street, what is most important is that the banking services of this country meet the needs of the country in all their aspects. Therefore it is imperative that this matter be discussed before the committee and that the minister very clearly outline government policy.
In this regard I refer briefly to the proposed banking legislation. I find it very difficult to understand how the government can justify a policy which actually discriminates against the Mercantile Bank, albeit it is United States owned at this time, when what was involved was merely the passing from one foreign ownership to another. It seems to me that rather than coming in the back door, harming our own reputation in international financial circles and impeaching the record of a parliament that has always been known for justice, we would have been far better served had we simply relied on that portion of section 53 which requires that the foreign ownership of shares in the Mercantile Bank or in any bank, including the Bank of Western Canada, be limited to 25 per cent. If such action could yet be taken it would be quite straightforward.
[DOT] (5:20 p.m.)
It is the responsibility of the government to draft banking legislation for each period of 10 years. It seems to me that the objective of making sure that the Mercantile Bank is serving the interests of the nation could have been reached by making the degree of foreign ownership very specific. Any discriminatory clauses in the bill should have been deleted, and I cannot see any excuse for them except to achieve the objective of Canadian ownership. However, this matter must be debated in greater detail following the committee hearings when the banking bill comes before the house. My remarks do not detract from the importance and urgency of dealing effectively with the problem that has arisen in connection with the Bank of Western Canada. Government policy must be adhered to; banking operations and institutions in Canada must serve first of all the interests of the Canadian people and their economy.
I now come to the mini-budget. I do not see why it should have been brought in. I know the minister said, either last fall or earlier in the summer, that a mini-budget would be needed because of dangerous inflationary elements developing in the economy. Between

The Budget-Mr. Thompson the time of that announcement and the minibudget conditions had changed greatly. The dangers of which he had forewarned us had begun to decline more rapidly than anticipated. He found it advisable to cancel action he had earlier intended taking.
The mini-budget concerns itself, therefore, with raising the money necessary to implement the guaranteed income provision for our senior citizens for the last three months of the fiscal year. The minister, it seems to me could have forgotten the mini-budget. He could have made a statement saying that the inflationary dangers in the economy had abuted to the point where it was not necessary to take special measures. He could have left the implementation of the extra tax for the next budget, which cannot now be far distant. The surplus in the old age security fund was more than enough to takecare of any expenditure necessary for the implementation of the guaranteed annual income for the first three months. In any event, payments to our senior citizens under the guaranteed income plan will not be made until March although they will be retroactive until January 1. It seems to me that this debate is redundant.
The minister decided to increase the income tax and the sales tax. As I said before, I commend the minister for making clear to the Canadian people that there is no secret source of government funds, that the only way money will be obtained, unless it is desired to increase deficit borrowing, is from the taxpayer's pocket. Because the increase in income tax does not really affect those in the low income brackets, that increase was the most logical way to collect the extra money.
I cannot agree with the decision to increase the sales tax by 1 per cent. Already our cost of living has risen so much, and is continuing to rise, that any increase in the cost of the things necessary for every-day living should be avoided. The minister argued that the 1 per cent increase in sales tax on certain items is not much and that the extra tax was a simple method to raise the additional income. The increase in sales tax from 11 per cent to 12 per cent does not mean an increased cost of just 1 per cent with respect to those items on which it is charged. The escalation of cost is more than that.
Before the house reassembled in the new year I took it on myself to investigate what the effect of the 1 per cent increase in sales tax would be in the wholesale grocery business with regard to those things normally sold in food stores. I came away with a sheaf


of letters. I will not burden the house by going over them in detail but will mention a few.
I found that the increase in the cost of powdered milk was exactly 5 per cent. Wholesale companies after January 1 were charging 5 per cent more for powdered milk than they had charged before that time. The price increase for condensed milk ranged from 5 per cent to 9 per cent. Certain other standard brand products increased in price at the wholesale level by 8 per cent or more. Cooking oil, for example, rose by a fantastic 35 per cent. To be specific, a case of 12 cans of vegetable oil which sold before January 1 at $5.61 increased to $7.60. This increase cannot be attributed wholly to the 1 per cent sales tax increase; nevertheless the excuse for raising the price was the sales tax increase, and part of the increased price was owing to the sales tax increase. I found that for many items sold in food stores-I will not enumerate them all-the price increases varied almost without exception from 5 to 8 per cent, the excuse for raising prices being the 1 per cent increase in sales tax.
This was at the wholesale level. The retail level had not entered the picture and neither in many instances had the jobber. The effect of the increased taxation has been to increase costs, to escalate costs at the various levels. The greatest single problem facing us now is the escalation in the cost of living.
In 1966 we had more strikes in more vital areas than ever before. Never before had labour demanded the large increases it demanded in 1966. With the cost of living going up, if workers are to maintain the standard of living they had previously had they will have to have more money to spend. So the struggle for increased wages goes on.
Recently I talked to an employer who has probably not more than a dozen employees. He had spoken to his employees during 1966 and told them over and over again that to demand more wages would further spiral the cost of living ever higher. He tried to show them that by demanding more wages they would defeat their own purpose and not until costs could be kept down could they expect to control the cost of living. He said to me, "I cannot again face my employees with that story again; in 1967 their standard of living will be lower than in 1966 unless their earning power is increased."
That is the situation. The problem is so acute that we in the Social Credit party contend it cannot continue. Unless something is

The Budget-Mr. Thompson
This is the danger I see in our present policy. Somehow or other we have managed to slow down our productivity while at the same time insisting on developing government budgets to the extent that half of what Canadians now earn is used merely to pay for the cost of government. That is a precarious situation in which to place ourselves.
It is said we have inflation in Canada. There is no inflation of money. We are short of money. In fact, one of the problems today on the whole international scene is that the world is short of money. Yet money is something which man makes and which man has the ability to control. Its purpose, basically, is to enable the distribution of goods and services, though it must also supply a standard of measurement and a means of storing wealth. One of the greatest needs facing this country today, in fact the greatest need which faces the whole free world today, is the introduction of a new system of monetary units which will reaffirm the fundamental purpose for which money was intended in the first place, that is, distribution. It is wrong to say there is inflation of money in Canada. There is not.
A previous speaker talked about the failure of Canadians to invest their savings in the development of Canada. That is true. The total amount held in savings accounts in Canada today is something in excess of $10 billion. If half of that sum were used for the development of our resources, for the expansion of our industry, we would not need the foreign capital we need today. For some reason Canadian people lack the confidence to invest their savings in the development of the resources of their country. Consequently it is necessary to depend on capital from the hands of foreigners who apparently have more confidence in Canada than we do ourselves as Canadians.
[DOT] (5:40 p.m.)
But the responsibility there, Mr. Speaker, falls back on government because unless government can set a climate, unless government can provide the incentive, unless our productivity does increase faster than the cost of government, then we shall continue to find ourselves in the position in which we are now. It is called inflation. It is not an inflation of money. It is an inflation of prices. It is an inflation of government expenditures. It is an inflation of the cost of everything we buy to the extent that Canadians, after paying taxes, do not have enough left to spend on those

things which are produced for their own needs. This is the real problem with which we are faced. Unless the Minister of Finance and his financial policies can move toward correcting this thing in some way which we are failing to do at the present time, the economy of Canada is in for trouble.
The Minister of Finance must be concerned about the problem of adjusting taxes, and there are several areas he must consider in this respect. Perhaps a little timely advice, whether he gives heed to it or not, is in order. In my opinion it is time we called a halt to the increase of government expenditures and a corresponding halt to tax increases. If we do not call a halt to the present trend of things, if the federal government does not set the pattern for provincial and municipal governments in this regard, then government expenditure is going to spiral faster than the increase in income and the increase of productivity in this country and the inflationary problem, which is one of prices, is going to get worse rather than better.
It seems to me that one of the first steps which must be taken is to call a halt to the increase in government expenditure. We have watched and listened with interest to the proceedings of the special committee on consumer prices. There is no doubt this committee is doing good work. But as I have observed and read some of the presentations made before that committee it seemed to me that the real cause of the increase in the cost of living was being neglected.
I think the number one cause of the increase in the cost of living is the tremendous increase in taxes because taxation compounds itself at its various levels, as we have seen with the 1 per cent sales tax increase. Tax increases are the first villain in the cost of living spiral. The second cause is the tremendous cost of usury and interest. We are living today in a debt economy, on a time payment, pay tomorrow, consumer purchasing basis, and unless we can do something to reduce the cost of usury we are not going to correct the problem. It is not a question of packaging or of somebody making too much profit or too high wages. The first cause is the increase in the cost of government and the second is the run away cost of usury and interest.
The government must give a lead in this matter. I simply cannot understand the government's policy with respect to the proposed banking legislation, which would free the rate of interest. It seems to me that what is required is a ceiling on the cost of interest.
February 6, 1967

particularly as it relates to consumer credit buying. We should lower the cost of interest from the top instead of taking the ceiling off and letting it rise from the bottom. By taking the ceiling off we are not going to reduce the cost of interest so far as the consumers of Canada are concerned.
Second, Mr. Speaker, I think it is imperative that in laying out his plans for his next budget the Minister of Finance should firmly establish priorities in the area of welfare. At the present time on the federal level approximately 35 per cent of everything we pay in taxes to the federal government is spent in the area of welfare. Out of 12 million Canadians who are 20 years of age or more, 5.5 million are actually receiving direct payments from government at this time. This is a situation which is extremely difficult to manage so far as federal budgets are concerned, but unless we are able to establish the priorities we are going to be in trouble, if we are not already in serious trouble.
There is no doubt in my mind that the first priority in the field of welfare is education. Unless we can provide educational facilities that will train the young people of today for the environment in which they will be making a living, and unless we can finance the retraining of older people who are no longer working in the professions or jobs in which they were originally trained, then we shall be failing them in their efforts to earn their own living. Today when the emphasis is on health and welfare it seems to me that we have our priorities reversed.
I realize that my time is just about finished, Mr. Speaker, but I have one or two other points I would like to make if I have permission to do so.

speechtext:
Thank you very much, Mr. Speaker. I think it is the responsibility of the Minister of Finance, as the member of the government responsible for financial and tax policies, to take a careful look at our present taxation structure in order to eliminate any inequitable taxes which are restricting the growth of the economy. The province of Alberta has taken a lead in this regard by eliminating an inequitable tax, succession duties. This principle applies to the gift tax as well. Here again the federal government
The Budget-Mr. Thompson should take a lead in eliminating this type of tax in consultation with the provinces, because certainly it is doing nothing but discouraging the investment of Canadian savings in Canada.
I do not have sufficient time to talk about many other areas where taxes are restrictive instead of expansionist, but as my closing point may I say it is also necessary and imperative that the national income be equalized with the total market values of consumer goods and services. This is a subject with which I will deal on another occasion, but for the moment suffice it to say I have statistics which show the pattern for the last 50 years. It is one in which the amount of income that the Canadian people earn in all of their different activities and have in their own pockets to buy consumer goods is not equal to the market value of that which is produced in consumer goods and services. Until the national income is equalized with the total market value of consumer goods and services we shall continue to have the debtor economy we have now. There is no alternative for it, and here again I think it is the responsibility of the Minister of Finance to do something in this regard in connection with banking legislation and monetary policies for which he is responsible. The debt building policies of government and consumers are not only wrong but they are leading us to national and personal bankruptcy. This has already been evident in 1966.
I would close by saying that tight money and higher taxes are not the answer to our present situation. Until we have fiscal and economic policies that will encourage the development of our national resources by Canadians, so that the productivity of our economy will exceed the actual increase in the growth rate of government expenditures, we shall continue to find ourselves as we are this year, unable to meet the logical needs of the Canadian people. There is no clearer example of this problem than our failure this year to have sufficient money in circulation to permit the construction industry of the country to build the homes that Canadians need. So, Mr. Speaker, I hope that the minister in finalizing his plans for his coming budget will give heed to some of these things, which are not my ideas but are the very facts of the economy, in order to bring about a policy to deal more effectively with these problems.

February 6, 1967
The Budget-Mr. Aiken

Mr. Speaker, in rising to speak on the supplementary budget a couple of months before the annual budget is due, I ask why this budget to announce these two tax increases was brought in when it was. I think that the impact of the old age security supplement would not already be felt before another budget could be brought in. Someone has said that the minister brought in a tax increase contemporaneously with the old age pension supplement to teach us a lesson that welfare costs money. This is indeed a lofty approach and flatters the minister unduly.
I do not generally quote newspapers and will not do so now. I will say, however, that the Vancouver Province in an editorial dated December 21 last year, set forth the proposal that this was the reason the minister brought in his budget when he did. Others said that it was not so much to teach us a lesson but rather that the minister had to face the economic fact that an increase in spending must be met by an immediate increase in taxation. This is a view held by the Toronto Telegram. Another newspaper expressed the opinion that the increase in the sales tax actually will help recover part of the pension increase

from the very people who will receive it, that is, from the pensioners as well as everyone else. This is only partly true and is not completely fair to the minister. Undoubtedly, however, that will be part of the effect. None of these approaches is entirely true. I am sure that neither the country, nor the members in the house, nor the minister's colleagues would benefit from or appreciate or require to be taught a lesson about economics in this manner.
The minister's political experience has been sufficient for him to know that the imposition of taxes just for the purpose of teaching people a lesson is not singularly appreciated. So far as facing economic facts is concerned, if we were to have a supplementary budget every time the government increased its spending we would have a continuous budget debate and hardly any legislation. Did we have a supplementary budget when the actual cost of Expo, for example, went up? Did we have a supplementary budget when the Canada Pension Plan bill came in last year which resulted in substantial additional spending?
