Did we have a supplementary budget to meet the extra costs as a result of the skyrocketing inflation and the increase in government spending? Perhaps the minister would answer that. I think not. But herein lies the answer. We all know the story of the straw that broke the camel's back. We know that the cost of government has grown and grown until the limit has been reached.
Just as the government was about to add the last straw the Minister of Finance snatched it away triumphantly protesting that we could not let our elderly break the camel's back and that we should ourselves carry the load of this extra straw. The minister knew that the Canadian people would gladly carry this little extra load on behalf of our senior citizens and that at the same time the camel would not break down. So our economy goes on carrying the load of the government's spending until the next straw comes by. I wonder whether the minister will find such a good excuse under similar circumstances the next time to pick off that next straw? I suppose we shall see what happens by the time the budget rolls around in a couple of months, but regardless of the reason let us not be led to think that the old age supplements were the whole cause of these two tax increases.
February 6, 1967

With otherwise healthy government, financing these tax increases could have been absorbed in other ways and without an additional budget. I think this is the fundamental matter which we must examine. If government spending had not accumulated to the point that it has, this additional load could have easily been carried. I think it is unfair that we should place on the old age pension supplement the sole cause for the tax increases that we are now considering.
This leads to another matter. Why do we find increasingly anxious attention being paid to our financial institutions at the present time? Canada's long-term financial prospects are excellent. The country at the present time could be described as being nervous. There is a lack of confidence because no firm businesslike action or legislation has been forthcoming from the government to meet the current problems. The cost of living continues to increase rapidly. While there are some increases in long-term credit, shortterm credit is in very short supply. This is what we need for our day by day operations.
How many royal commissions, parliamentary committees and other boards of inquiry will the government continue to set up to look into questions on which it should make a decision itself? Just recently I have had cause to raise some question concerning the number of committees which are sitting to look into an immense number of problems, many of which could be placed directly before the government and action taken. While these committees are valuable in a great many cases, I think they are abused in many other cases when they are used to help the government put off making a definite decision in respect of some of these important problems.
I see it is six o'clock, Mr. Speaker. I believe something further is to be announced.

Mr. Speaker, at the adjournment I was discussing the situation of the financial institutions of this country. I believe we recognize that the government will either
The Budget-Mr. Aiken have to cut tax expenditures or increase taxes in order to restore confidence in the economy. The last controversy over the Bank of Western Canada, following other difficulties with regard to financial institutions in Canada, will merely add fuel to the fire. Regardless of the reasons for the dispute, it has come at a particularly unfortunate time. The fact that the issue has been raised by Mr. James Coyne, who seems to have a penchant for public controversy, will certainly cause many hon. members some scepticism. However, his allegations should be fully investigated to ensure that the objects of this banking institution are properly carried out.
To come back for a moment to the budget debate, I would say we have been puzzled by the apparent reluctance of government members up to this time to take part in the debate. Here is the opportunity for many of the members of the Liberal party to discuss the important matters of the economy of this country. We read in the press from time to time about the lack of opportunity for private members on the government side of the house to speak out. Having been a member on the government side for some years, I recognize the lack of opportunity in many cases when they have so many experts sitting in front of them to discuss almost all fields. But here is the opportunity, during the budget debate, for some of these monumental expositions to be made.
However, Mr. Speaker, we have had four consecutive opposition members speaking on this budget debate without any government members seeming to clamour for the opportunity to speak great words in favour of the budget. I understand that there are one or two government members now ready, willing and anxious to present their views; but it has been a matter of some bewilderment to us that they have not sought to speak before. Perhaps they are too embarrassed by this unnecessary budget to take part in the debate, and merely want to get it over with and hope the government may come up with something more vital, something more meaningful for them to discuss. Perhaps it is difficult for the government members to explain a general tax increase at a time when the economy needs some encouragement, rather than discouragement.
I shall not reiterate what I said before the dinner hour, but it seems that this budget was an unnecessary exposition so close to the time for a regular budget, when a general tax increase could have been applied. I think it

February 6, 1967
The Budget-Mr. Aiken was something the minister felt he had to do for the expedience of the moment, and now wishes he had left undone until a later date. However, I do not want to delay the budget debate for that reason. I believe it was unnecessary; it was ill-timed and left a cloud on the older people of this country; it left the general impression with the public that it was only to provide the old age security supplement that additional taxes had to be raised. As I indicated previously, this was not the sole reason, and if there had been a properly managed economy it could have absorbed this latest burden on the taxpayers of the country.
[DOT] (8:10 p.m.)
The budget debate is normally a time to air complaints. While this is a fairly narrow budget, I have one complaint that I want to raise at this time in connection with budget matters. Being a member from a rural riding it bothers me considerably. It relates to the administration of unemployment insurance in rural areas. One of the things that a person living in a rural area is required to do when he applies for unemployment insurance is to prove that he is willing and able to accept employment, and that he is available for work. The Unemployment Insurance Commission has taken this to mean that a person who wishes to draw unemployment insurance must not limit the place of employment, the wages, or the type of job that he is prepared to accept. Time after time people in rural areas receive notices of disqualification because they have said that they find it difficult to work outside the community in which they reside. However, if they do state in their applications that they wish to work only within the immediate area of residence, they are disqualified by their own words.
To make it worse, they are often encouraged by the Unemployment Insurance Commission to state exactly where and when they will accept a job. If they say that they will not accept a job at a certain place 15 miles away, they may be disqualified on the ground that they have refused a job which, really, was never offered to them. This is most difficult for those people who have been raised, have worked and lived in a rural or an isolated community. The Unemployment Insurance Commission says: "You may have lived and worked there but we cannot get you a job there, so you had better go somewhere else." There may be reasons for it under some circumstances, but it is difficult in many cases for men to travel 30, 40 or 50 miles when they

do not have transportation, when they are out of a job and when they cannot afford to maintain two homes.
If it is difficult for men, it is all the more difficult for women who either work part time to supplement the family income, or even support a family because of the inability of the husband to do so or because of his absence. And yet such a woman living in a rural area is told that she has to leave the community and go somewhere else to find employment.
Of course this is absolutely impossible. I run across this time after time and I take this opportunity to raise the issue and to ask that the unemployment insurance regulations be applied somewhat more reasonably to people in rural areas. It might be that we have a particularly difficult office in our area but I have heard the same complaint from other hon. members. I hope the government will give some thought to a more reasonable application of the Unemployment Insurance Act.
Mr. Speaker, my time has just about expired. I hope that before the budget debate is concluded we will hear some hon. members on the government side explain how they can justify the imposition of the tax in question at a time when perhaps it could have been avoided. I hope they will explain why the apparent burden of the increase in taxes was cast upon the older people of this country. We know very well that while the granting of benefits to the older people was a factor in the increase in taxation, it was not the only factor. If the economy of the country had been in proper shape, if we had not been spending money recklessly and going into debt, we would have been able to absorb this increase instead of raising the tax at the time when we decided to give the old people a supplement. In this way we have burdened them with this increase.
I am sure the minister knew that the people of Canada would accept an additional tax, but I do not think we should be under the illusion that a supplement to the older people was the whole reason for a tax increase at this time. We have burdened ourselves to the point where a tax increase would have been necessary anyway. We may have to have another increase in the regular budget. It seems to me that the minister is approaching this matter in a piecemeal way and is trying to cast the burden of his difficulty on as broad a spectrum of the population as possible.
February 6, 1967

Mr. Speaker, as the hon. member for Parry Sound-Muskoka (Mr. Aiken) has pointed out, this is the opportunity for private members to express their opinions on financial matters, and on other matters generally that are of concern to them. I am seeking to use this opportunity for that purpose and I am speaking as a private member representing Kootenay East. I think it is true that despite the fulminations of the members of the opposition, the budget speech as outlined by the minister has met with general approval. It is true that no one relishes a tax increase, but on the other hand those who are benefiting-and some of them have been mentioned by the hon. member for Parry Sound-Muskoka-certainly smile with approbation when it means an increase in grants.
I think the hollowness of the invective of the opposition can best be disclosed by turning back a few pages of Hansard to the debate on the act which provided for a supplement to old age security. Of course at that time it was a call for higher grants, while today it is a call for a reduction in taxes. This reminds me of the sage advice that was given to me when I was a rookie member of parliament-admittedly quite a number of years ago-that a successful politician never votes for a tax bill or against a grant.
Generally speaking I think that governments must face up to the horrible facts of life and be ever mindful of the Scottish politician's advice which is as follows:
They'll dom soon forget what you've already gie 'em, but they'll remember for a long time what you ain't gie 'em yet.
While it is not my purpose to criticize the imposition of higher income taxes on certain groups of taxpayers and an increase in the sales tax, I do offer a suggestion which I believe to be fair and reasonable. To some members of the house it will be very unpopular, but I know that others will recognize that deep down in their hearts they find it acceptable, although they might not be prepared to admit it. I know also that it will be unpopular with a large and what I believe to be a preferred section of our population. It will indeed constitute a severe criticism of the economic philosophy of my friends, but I hope they will take it in the best sense, namely that it is a question of principle and that I believe it to be in the best interest of all Canadians.

The Budget-Mr. Byrne
I am referring to the removal of the special tax privilege enjoyed by co-operative enterprises and credit unions. Had this special tax incentive, based as it is on no sound economic or fiscal theory, been removed decades ago when co-operatives first emerged from the local self-help status on which they were founded, no new taxes would have been necessary at this time.
[DOT] (8:20 p.m.)
The co-operative movement, as it chooses to be called, is nothing more nor less than corporate enterprise enjoying the benefits of $3 billion worth of business each year in Canada. Co-operatives have become a corporate colossus in competitive enterprise, but with a difference. Co-operative profits are almost completely exempt from income tax. Their competitive advantage at the expense of the corporate and personal taxpayer may be simply stated. A corporate enterprise, in order to undertake a $1 million expansion program must have first earned $2 million in excess of a reasonable return on invested capital. One half of the corporate profit, or 52 per cent, must first be handed over to government, its sleeping but avaricious partner in business. The co-operative, on the other hand, need earn only $1 million, declare the full amount in patronage dividends and retain all or nearly all as capital for reinvestment purposes. The co-operative has no sleeping partner who demands 52 per cent of the corporate earnings.
Since the beginning of the industrial revolution, the eggheads have tended to look upon a corporate enterprise as a menace to society. Anyone who dares to defend corporate enterprise is one virtually living in sin. I believe, and sincerely believe, it is the benefits of corporate enterprise, operating under a democratic free enterprise system, that has provided for us on the North American continent the highest standard of living in the world, and in Canada the most comprehensive social welfare program in the world. Certainly, nothing I saw during my recent visit to the Union of Soviet Socialist Republics altered, even in the minutest detail, this long held conviction.

Thank you, Mr. Speaker. The price index reveals that the cost of fertilizer has decreased over the period mentioned. The 1965 index shows farm machinery at 284, a rise of 184 points; building material 405, a rise of 305 points; feed 230, a rise of 130 points; seed 212, a rise of 112 points, and fertilizer 180 for a rise of only 80 points. In the light of these figures, was there real justification for co-operatives, short of a genuine profit motive, entering into the fertilizer production field?
On a relatively small scale tailored to growing western demand, Cominco has developed the first iron and steel production industry in western Canada, but it was, and still remains, a by-product of fertilizer processing. The expansion of this embryonic industry, therefore, is contingent upon continuing fertilizer production and expansion at the Kimberley plant. Here iron tailings, of which there are many million tons in storage and other thousands produced daily, are roasted to produce sulphuric acid and iron calcine. But it is a costly process consuming vast quantities of electrical energy. Sulphuric acid is the main re-agent in all phosphate fertilizer manufacture.
While the production of fertilizer by this process may stand alone under normal competitive conditions, production of iron and steel could not. In other words, it appears to me that the continuation and expansion of the steel industry in the Kootenays is directly related to the production and marketability of fertilizer. Fertilizer production at this time is an extremely marginal operation and cost of money is a major determining factor.
February 6, 1967

The Budget-Mr. McCleave
Any suggestion of a substantial reduction in price, even far less than the 35 per cent proposed by Mr. Gibbins, and made possible only through tax privileges tantamount to a direct subsidy, would simply eliminate corporate enterprise from the market. Such a prospect seriously jeopardizes the economy of the Kootenays and the welfare of hundreds of my constituents.
I ask hon. members, therefore to consider seriously everything I have said. Would it not be appropriate, in this centennial year, to change our tax laws to make them equally applicable to all-to share the tax burden without special privilege to any group?

Robichaud, who happens to be the premier of New Brunswick. The government's tight money policy lies particularly hard upon Atlantic Canada, and questions have been raised by the return to the federal government of the hon. member for Davenport (Mr. Gordon). The Budget-Mr. McCleave
I suppose that under the policies of the government those with one point of view hold the fort for a particular time, and those with another point of view hold it at another time, thus trying to beguile the voters. But the return of the hon. member for Davenport to the cabinet was aptly pronounced upon in a recent editorial in the Montreal Gazette, from which I quote in part that it-
-recalls what old Dr. Samuel Johnson said about a man who had married for the second time. "It was," said Dr. Johnson, "the triumph of hope over experience."

speechtext:
Old, but none the less true. Why did the hon. member return to the cabinet? We know that in mid November a number of reverse going away, farewell dinners were held for him saying, "After all, don't go, Walter." Then came the announcement by the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) that the lost sheep had returned to the fold.
We recall when he left on November 10, 1965, after an electoral event which could only be counted a disaster by his own party. When he met with his fellow colleagues in the cabinet two days after that event and said, "I am going to resign because I gave you bad advice," to his dismay they accepted his offer, right on the spot.
My own inference from what happened recently-I was not there and nobody has blabbed yet-is simply that the Prime Minister decided it would be unprofitable and unwise to open up the Davenport seat for a by-election. Therefore he was faced with two alternatives, neither one very palatable. One was to let the hon. member resign from the house and have a by-election; the other one was to have him back in the cabinet. There was no middle ground, and he chose what was best in the interests of the Liberal party for the time being, whether it was best for the country or not.
Again I quote from the Montreal Gazette editorial:
In view of the record, there can be little enthusiasm for Mr. Pearson's decision to place Mr. Gordon at the head of a committee to study the implications of foreign ownership and control of Canadian industry. This happens to be the field in which Mr. Gordon, when last holding office, held the most extreme opinions and was well on the way of doing the most damage.
Such policies as he supported brought protests from the Canadian Chamber of Commerce, the Canadian Manufacturers' Association, the Canadian Institute of Chartered Accountants, and from many other sources concerned with practical business.
February 6, 1967

The Budget-Mr. McCleave
To that distinguished list we could add the former president of BRINCO and Rio Tinto, the Minister of Trade and Commerce, (Mr. Winters) who has no aptitude for swallowing the Gordonian philosophy.
What has the Prime Minister done with the shadow minister of finance? I suggest he has done this: He has appointed him in charge of a very important study, a gentleman who has his verdict ready now and is simply going to go around and scout up such facts, and the blessings of such colleagues as he can muster to the cause to support him in that verdict.
It may be said of the Minister of Trade and Commerce that he at least has sense enough to stay away from such a dubious undertaking. It also allows him to go forth with a straight face and let it appear that nothing really has happened by the return of the hon. member for Davenport to the cabinet, clutching his carpetbag of strange and narrow, isolationist, fiscal policies.
I now wish to deal with the budget, Mr. Speaker, and concentrate on its sins of omission. There is one that really stands out. Surely when we study the problems that today baffle Canadians, the most serious problem we have is the failure to come to grips with soaring prices. From the Third Annual Review of the Economic Council of Canada, 1966, quoting from page 191, I point to the paragraph where recommendations included:
[DOT] (9:10 p.m.)
To achieve a more satisfactory reconciliation of economic goals, the main policy "levers" must be complemented by policies whose primary focus is the supply rather than the demand side of the economy. Among these are effective manpower and other policies to encourage the flow of available resources into their highest and most remunerative uses, and to help relieve the economic pressure points which are in part responsible for the appearance of excessive price and cost increases before the economy has reached its potential path.
Later on in the recommendations point 9 might be drawn to the attention of the minister. It reads in part as follows:
It is more than ever important that effective measures be taken to increase productivity at all stages of food production and distribution.
This is all good fodder for the Minister of Finance; and all of this, by the way, was available to that minister some weeks before the budget was presented. The following is a quotation from page 199:
Among the required measures are an important range of supply-oriented policies, including those designed to improve productivity, to strengthen competition, to facilitate adjustments to technological and other change, and to increase manpower training and mobility.

Giving him a few marks and some Christian generosity for some of those points, I still say that the minister has failed absolutely to come to grips with the most important suggestions made by the Economic Council of Canada in that particular report. Instead, some of the excursions and forays of the government into this field smack more of a public relations technique than one of honest and sound administration.
At page 181 of this Third Annual Review a press release of the President of the Privy Council is quoted fairly extensively. This press release dealt with the fact that the Economic Council had been asked to carry on a major investigation in the general area of reasonable price stability. The point I make is that the Economic Council of Canada did not find very much about the terms of reference from the order in council that was passed, but found them from a press release issued by a member of the cabinet. This is one of the most extraordinary things, I think, which one could see in government, even government by press release such as we have now.
Well, sir, I will very quickly conclude. I would have preferred that the budget had dealt not only with the particular point of price stability, something which is bedevilling Canadians, but also the matter of a higher exemption in the income tax. If we agree with the Senate committee on aging, that $1,260 should be a minimum for our old people, we would probably also say that $1,260 should be a minimum for our younger people and that therefore $1,260 should be the exemption for any one person in Canada. I think to that some people would be inclined to reply Q.E.D.-quod erat demonstrandum.
This is another thing which should have been included in the budget in order to help the young married people of this nation who must go out and make capital expenditures for furniture and accommodation in order to get their marriages and eventually their families under way. I think the budget has fallen down sadly in that regard. For these reasons, and because the Minister of Finance (Mr. Sharp) has proposed to impose taxes at this particular time when taxes do not appear to be necessary, I support the amendment and will reject this budget.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to intervene in this budget debate to discuss a few matters which I consider most important and which I would hope the government would

adopt as policy in this centennial year. Last September the Minister of Finance moved that certain matters with regard to the cost of living be referred to the joint committee of the Senate and House of Commons on consumer credit. The committee was asked to look into the causes of the rapid rise in the cost of living with regard to consumer items and report and make recommendations. After many sittings during the months of September, October, November and December the committee issued an interim report in the middle of December in which it made very significant recommendations.
At this time I feel obliged to take strong exception to some of the remarks made by my colleague the hon. member for Kootenay East (Mr. Byrne), because I feel that his opinions do not, according to my understanding, reflect the thinking on this side of the house with regard to credit unions and co-operatives. It always has been my humble feeling that co-operatives were a means whereby small businessmen-the farmer, the fisherman and the consumer-got together, through a co-operative exercise, to make it possible for a man to be the master of his own destiny, to use the words of Dr. M. M. Cody, the great pioneer of co-operatives in Nova Scotia for whom I have always had the greatest respect.

Mr. Speaker, during the hearings of the committee on consumer credit several witnesses appeared who recommended, not that the role of the co-operatives be restricted, but that it be increased. Several witnesses who appeared before the committee suggested there should be a federal act to govern co-operatives. This is something which we do not have at present. This would help the co-operatives help people through cooperative action, on a broader scale than they can now. At present they are restricted to the provincial co-operative acts. The co-operative federation for many years has been recommending that there be a federal co-operatives act. It may be, after we have studied this matter more in the committee, that we may recommend to the government that such a bill be introduced.
The Budget-Mr. Allmand
It is significant that the Stewart Royal Commission in 1959 recommended that there be a federal co-operatives act, but so far that recommendation has not been accepted either by the previous government or by this government. I think it was in 1906 or 1908 that a Liberal government introduced into this house a bill to establish a federal co-operatives act, but the bill was defeated in the Senate after it had been passed by the House of Commons.
There were other important recommendations in the interim report of the committee on consumer credit (prices). One of the most important recommendations was that we establish a department of consumer affairs. Many members have asked why it is necessary that we have a department of consumer affairs. They say it is important that the consumer be protected but they ask why is it necessary that we have a department and a minister to do it. Of course it is important that the public's interest be protected, and I think it also is important that we have a department and a minister whose sole responsibility is to be concerned with consumer problems and to initiate legislation to protect the consumer and help him with regard to the problems of the rising cost of living, inflation and so on.
Right now there are several statutes which are designed to protect the consumer, but these statutes presently are administered under five separate departments. They are under the Department of National Health and Welfare, the Department of Fisheries, the Department of Agriculture, the Department of the Registrar General and the Department of Finance. Although the statutes are fairly well administered under these departments, I think if we are to have co-ordination with regard to consumer affairs and the administration of these statutes they should be brought together under one ministry.
[DOT] (9:20 p.m.)
Another point is that most of these departments are concerned more with production, and the producer end of farming and fishing, than with the consumer who eventually buys the products of these industries. I hope that when the government introduces the speech from the throne in this centennial year a department of consumer affairs will be one of the items included in that speech.
There were other recommendations in the interim report on consumer affairs which are also very important. These were recommendations to help and protect consumers. One
February 6, 1967

The Budget-Mr. Allmand recommendation was that there should be more and better grading processes of the different products sold on the Canadian market. There was also a recommendation that there should be labelling and packaging of products which would provide more information for consumers as to the contents.
It was found by the committee on consumer prices that one of the groups hardest hit by the inflation which took place between the middle of 1965 and the middle of 1966 were those persons on fixed incomes, and especially the pensioners. That is why we were so ready to welcome around Christmas the legislation of the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. MacEachen) increasing the old age pension by $30 a month and introducing the new concept of a guaranteed minimum income. I hope this guaranteed minimum income will be increased in the future, because although it is a worth while measure at the present time I think that as a guaranteed minimum income it is too low. But I appreciate the fact, and congratulate the Minister of Finance (Mr. Sharp) for this, that when we adopted this measure of social welfare he let it be known that we do not spend large sums of money on measures such as this without paying for them.
I accept what the minister said in this respect, namely that at this particular time the tax measures necessary to provide for the guaranteed minimum income were about as high as we could go, but I hope this income can be raised in the future. I also hope that this is only the beginning, and sooner or later this policy will be applied to other welfare measures such as family allowances, unemployment insurance and similar programs. I think we should maintain a guaranteed minimum income across the board for people who are unemployed, families, and so on, in addition to providing it to our old age pensioners.
The hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Mc-Cleave) mentioned the tax exemption. I support the suggestion that the exemption for people on pension be at least raised to $1,260, because at the present time the extra $500 exemption, as all hon. members know, applies only to those over 70 years of age. Under the new legislation there will be pensioners receiving $1,260 per year through the guaranteed minimum income program, and they will have to pay tax on $160. I do not think this is fair. I hope that in the budget to be presented later this year the minister will take steps to correct this situation.

Then I hope they would take steps to put that policy into effect. I congratulate the Department of Transport for-

certainly support all reasonable measures to help these maritime ports become more efficient and competitive.
The final matter I wish to raise this evening in the budget debate is that of air pollution. I raise this question also as a Montrealer because we had recently in that city a very difficult problem with air pollution. Again I know the government has taken certain initiatives in this respect, but because of the very great danger to Canadians I think the initiatives must be increased. I have here a quotation of Senator Robert F. Kennedy of New York. Senator Kennedy said that:
-air pollution in New York city is so acute that every year "old and young, rich and poor, athlete or infirm recluse ... breathes in 750 pounds of his own wastes".
I have another quotation of the words of Vice President Hubert Humphrey of the United States, who said:
More people are dying from emphysemawhich is a throat disease aggravated by air pollution-

than on the field of battle in Viet Nam-
I think that many of us, because we can go outside and breathe do not recognize the seriousness of this problem right now and believe we can put it off until some time in the future. But I think that if we do not do something now, in 1967, on a very large scale to combat air pollution, in a very few years we will be in very serious trouble, and then it may be too late to do very much about it.
[DOT] (9:30 p.m.)
So I would like to recommend strongly to the government that during Canada's centennial year it adopt what I think are three worth-while programs: first, that it take a serious look at the recommendations contained in the interim report of the committee on consumer prices; second, that it undertake a large scale and effective program on air pollution; and third, that it adopt a serious and positive policy with respect to winter navigation on the St. Lawrence.

Mr. Speaker, I believe that the budget which we are considering tonight is a good indication and reflection of the government's attitudes. I certainly hope that the hon. member for Kootenay East (Mr. Byrne) who loosed a diatribe against co-operatives such as has seldom been heard in the house, was not reflecting the government's views. The entire
The Budget-Mr. Saltsman budget suffers from defects which we exemplified in the speech made by the hon. member for Kootenay East. It showed a complete lack of concern for what is going on in the country and for the needs of the people of this country, and an excessive concern for maintaining the corporate power, which is already far too great. When we see a co-operative movement in existence, people banding together to try to find an alternative to this power structure, to try to reduce prices, and to insist on competition, it is disconcerting to find this kind of attitude in response. This is regrettable, especially as it comes from one so close to the government as is the parliamentary secretary.
In introducing his budget the Minister of Finance (Mr. Sharp) referred to it as a neutral budget. I think that the word "neutral" is too kind. Perhaps it should be called a "paralysed" budget, because this is what it reflects. It reflects a paralysis on the part of the government in dealing with the great and pressing problems of this country.
We have the problem of Canadian identity and nationalism, and what is the government doing about it? After having permitted this problem to develop throughout the years, all of a sudden it shows a sort of enthusiasm toward solving it. We see people running around in circles, establishing task forces and looking for answers. Royal commissions on this subject have been set up, many books have been written and I do not know how many investigations have taken place and opinions have been offered. However, now that we are faced with a crisis, a task force is being set up. I do not know what solutions this task force will bring, but I have very little hope that it will find solutions to our problems. If these solutions will consist in putting some kind of curb on United States ownership without examining the deep-rooted problems in the economic structure of Canada, then that task force will have been a complete failure and will have misled the Canadian people. I hope sincerely that it does come up with some answers although, judging from its actions and from its personnel, I do not have the kind of confidence which I wish I could have in this particular case.
The Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. Marchand) has been working very hard and, generally speaking, has been applauded for his efforts in the field of manpower. He has introduced a mobility program which, as we pointed out from the start, was
February 6. 1967

The Budget-Mr. Saltsman inadequate because it only touched the surface of the problem, because it was too restrictive in outlook, and because it depended on an entirely new set of ancillary conditions in order to prove its effectiveness. These ancillary conditions are not even being recognized by the Minister of Finance. The result is that the mobility program is a complete failure. The figures on this subject given to us by the Minister of Manpower and Immigration indicate this. One of the reasons for its failure is that we have not provided for the kind of housing that will be needed in those areas into which we attempt to move people. People cannot be moved into non-existing houses. They cannot be expected to move from one area of the country into another area in which housing is not available to them.
An effective immigration program cannot be established when the minister warns immigrants not to go to certain centres in Canada which are perhaps the centres which need them most. On the one hand an agency says to them: Come on over, we need you, we would like to have you, and on the other hand they are told to stay away because no houses are available for them. There is complete confusion and paralysis in terms of defining objectives and trying to achieve them.
An inflationary situation has developed in this country. We have seen the cost of living go up higher and faster than it has for a long time, and the first thing that happens under those circumstances is that the government suddenly forgets the grand words which it used in the Speech from the Throne when it said: "There will be a war on poverty. There will be an end to poverty in Canada. The dispossessed will be considered." We do not hear this any more because we have failed to control the inflationary process in this country and because of a lack of imagination in dealing with this problem. The grand design for our society has gone down the drain, and this budget reflects it. There is hardly a word in the budget about the kind of obligation which the government should have toward those who need the assistance of the government.
The government Is to blame to a large extent for allowing the interest rates to rise. The Minister of Finance even acknowledged some of his responsibility in this matter. We have started to put on the brakes elsewhere. The minute brakes are applied to the general economy it is the large regions in the country

where no brakes are required that suffer most, even in the most overheated circumstances. The disparity in income between prosperous regions in Canada and those who are trying to achieve that prosperity is still great. Where in this budget can the answer be found? Where is there even a recognition that such a problem exists in this country, recognition of the fact that an attitude which is appropriate to an economically viable section of Canada is certainly not appropriate to those areas which need development urgently and which could be developing at this time without adding anything to the problems of inflation or to the difficulties in controlling the cost of living? There is nothing dealing with this in the budget, not even an apparent awareness.

We have seen medicare sacrificed on the flimsiest of excuses. This was not done in this budget, but it was done in the previous budget and the minister could have corrected that in this budget. Medicare was thrown to the dogs, and why was it thrown to the dogs? There is not an economist in this country who will defend the minister when he says that medicare was inflationary, that medicare was really a serious problem with which he had to cope. The impression remains, and it is an impression I do not like to consider, but it is unavoidable, that the minister took this action to satisfy those companies which were so ably defended tonight by the hon. member for Kootenay East (Mr. Byrne). Perhaps his actions were a sop to these corporate giants who felt that the postponement of medicare was the kind of restraint this country needed.
February 6, 1967

This budget will go down as one of the most insensitive documents ever presented to this house. It is almost without justification in what has been done to convey the chastising image of the government. I believe we are rather fortunate in Canada in that scorpions and whips are rather rare, or perhaps the minister might have used them as the medium to impress upon the Canadian people the fact they have to pay for welfare services, that money does not grow on trees. This is a spurious argument. It has been repeatedly shown that these taxation measures were not necessary to pay for this kind of program.
I should like to read an editorial from the Toronto Star which I think puts the situation rather well. It carried the heading "The Budget: Moralism Through a Fog" and states:
Canada has found Its stern public moralist, its Cromwell of the treasury, in Finance Minister Mitchell Sharp.
If there was any real purpose behind last night's mini-budget except to point the moral lesson that new social security benefits must be paid for immediately. it was not evident in the facts and figures which Mr. Sharp himself gave ...
It is good of Mr. Sharp to care about our moral redemption. But it's an odd system of priorities for a minister of finance. We must hope the economy and the ill-housed can bear so much virtue, such Cromwellian zeal.
The minister and the government which I presume he represented in the presentation of his budget, had an opportunity to bring in social justice as something which should be brought in with pride and satisfaction, a sense of achievement, instead of representing it as a burden. I was interested in a speech the minister made on October 13 to the National Industrial Conference Board in which he gave his views on welfare services:
I am one of those who believe that these vital responsibilities are a proper burden to place equitably upon all of us in dividing the fruits of our increasing productivity which arises in a very large measure from joint efforts made by many.
This is the view of the minister and presumably the view of the government. Our sick are a burden; it is too bad they will not go away. Our elderly are a burden; it is too bad they grew old and have to be cared for. The fact that they worked all their lives to build this nation should not mean they are now a burden. The weak are a burden. The just society that we all seek has become a burden. What sort of philosophy is this for the government to have? What sort of budget is this that reflects this kind of attitude toward the whole problem of social justice in Canada? This budget is regressive, and it is
The Budget-Mr. Saltsman being called regressive by many. Except for a
small bow the minister made to progressiveness in raising the ceiling on the old age pension tax, the minister did not make any other obeisance.
I should like to quote from a column in the Toronto Star which gives the opinion of F. Gerald Townsend, a tax specialist and partner in the chartered accountancy firm of Thorne, Gunn, Helliwell and Christanson. Mr. Townsend said:
The increase in the maximum old age pension tax payment from $120 to $240 per year would mean an increase of 2 per cent to a person with a taxable income of $6,000 per year. However, to a person with a taxable income of $30,000, the increase would be only one half of one per cent.
In a similar way the increase in the federal sales tax from 11 to 12 per cent would bear more heavily by proportion on those with smaller incomes. This was direct violation of the principle of payment according to ability to pay.
If we were going to be chastised, then should not everyone be chastised equally or are some to be chastised more than others, especially those with lower incomes? Perhaps these people have been chastised more because they have lower incomes and deserve to be chastised more. Perhaps this is the attitude of the government. I should like to hear the minister defend his position before the Canadian people instead of adopting this surreptitious way of bringing in this philosophy through the back door. I feel he will find the Canadian people have ways of examining these proposals and evaluating them.
In the speech to which I referred the minister was talking about what a lucky country Canada is. I should like to quote his statement-
When before have men ever been able to look forward with confidence to such cumulative improvements? Where in the world, outside of a few lucky countries like our own, can one hope for so much?
It is true that we are a lucky country, and we have every right to hope for a great deal; but that hope does not appear likely to come to fruition as a result of the actions of this government. I should like to quote from the Second Annual Review of the Economic Council of Canada. They give some of the reasons this country has a right to expect something more than has been presented to us in this particular budget. I quote from page 61 of the report:
It is widely recognized that Canada has important natural resources in the form of minerals, petroleum, forests, fresh water and agricultural land. Historically, natural resources and their development and export have played an important 'role in
February 6, 1967

The Budget-Mr. Saltsman the development of particular regions of Canada and the timing and industrial composition of growth in the country as a whole.
The above considerations indicate that both the extent of capital facilities and the use of land and natural resources per person tend to operate in the direction of a higher level of productivity in Canada than in the United States. In combination with other factors, a large volume in capital, land and other natural resources may be very important elements in high levels of productivity, but they are not sufficient in themselves to assure the attainment of high productivity and high standards of living. Thus, the main explanation for the lower levels of Canadian incomes per employed person must lie in the differences in the quality of Canada's productive resources, and in the efficiency with which these productive resources are combined in the production process-that is, the scales of output, degrees of specialization, the attitudes and effectiveness of management and labour, and so forth.
Instead of "so forth" we could have said, "because of government policies." In Canada, we have the greatest opportunity to be the most affluent nation in the world. Instead of that, Mr. Speaker, with all these advantages and opportunities, our level is about 25 per cent lower than that of the United States.
[DOT] (9:50 p.m.)
It is not that our people do not work as hard. I think we see instances where they work just as hard as it is possible for any group of people to work. But without proper policies and the proper involvement of the government in the affairs of the nation in order to get the maximum use of our resources, our capital and our labour, we cannot achieve these levels that we are entitled to expect.
The most indefensible attitude of this government is when it talks about productivity, congratulates itself on its level of productivity and what it has done to achieve it. As we look at the budget, Mr. Speaker, where do we see a single measure which indicates we are going to do something to improve productivity? There is only a negative measure. Perhaps the inference is that if we do not have a universal old age pension in Canada we will have productivity, which is a fallacy.
On the question of sales tax, Mr. Speaker, is there any indication that the sales tax can be used in a selective manner to ensure productivity? We see that not at all. The very items which are needed to assist productivity are those which the minister is insisting upon taxing.
As to investment policy, Mr. Speaker, is there any direction or guidance given to the country in this budget? Is there any indication Of the role which is played by social


capital in improving productivity? Are there any measures in relation to the research programs which are so badly needed in this country to improve our productivity? Where are the measures to rationalize Canadian industry, which almost every expert now agrees is one of the central problems facing this nation? There is none of these measures, Mr. Speaker. But there is moralizing.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I should like to say that what this country needs is a little less moralizing from the minister and his government and a few more ideas about how to run the nation. This budget is a document of omissions of those things which should have been done. It says nothing to the Canadian people. It offers no hope to those looking for a government to provide a sense of direction to the nation. It offers no challenge to the people of Canada to rally around ideas being developed by the government, so as to create the great society we all seek. It does none of these things, and for that reason has to be condemned.
The minister would have been far better off never to have introduced such a budget. He has displayed the nakedness and poverty of the government's program. It is almost an insult to bring in a budget of this type. The prideful minister said he was going to bring in a budget and he brought one in, even though the reasons for a budget no longer existed. The minister should have maintained his pride by bringing in a budget of a positive nature, one which would have encouraged the economy and spurred the nation on to those goals that it seeks.
In view of the lateness of the hour, Mr. Speaker, I would be very pleased to accept the question the parliamentary secretary seemed so keen on putting. I see he has had his question answered during the course of my speech, and I am very pleased that I have been able to anticipate the problem that was in his mind. I hope he has listened carefully to what has been said and will be able to convey these thoughts to the minister when he sees him.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am glad to have the opportunity to speak for a few minutes about a question which is important to all members of the house who have any feelings for their fellow-men. On January 26 I asked the following question of the right hon. Prime Minister, to be found at page 12260 of Hansard:
My question is based on a statement contained in a question asked of the Prime Minister by the hon. member for Bow River on January 24 in which he said, as recorded at page 12159 of Hansard:
"To review my question, it referred to $50,000 of aid to Viet Nam of which ninety per cent was going to North Viet Nam, to the Viet Cong, for purposes other than to assist civilian victims."
Has the Prime Minister received a letter from Dr. A. M. Inglis, chairman of the committee on Canadian aid for Viet Nam civilians, which committee, I might mention, is sponsored by a number of Canadians including the leader of our party and the hon. member for Kootenay West, which outlines the facts with respect to the distribution of this aid-
There was more questioning and the hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Woolliams) asked supplementary questions. I say that the lusty member for Bow River had been misinformed. I expect the parliamentary secretary this evening will be better informed than the hon. member was when he asked the question.
I have in my hand a letter written by Major General A. E. Wrinch, C.B.E., C.D.,
12722	COMMONS DEBATES	February 6, 1967
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion National Commissioner of the Canadian Red Cross Society, addressed to A. M. Inglis, Esq.,
M.	D., F.R.C.S. (C), Canadian Aid for Viet Nam Civilians, P.O.B. 2543, Vancouver 3, B.C. I wish to quote a couple of paragraphs from the letter:
During my recent visit to Geneva on League of Red Cross Societies business, I took the opportunity of discussing this subject with Mr. Roger Gallopin, Executive Director of the I.C.R.C. Mr. Gallopin stated that the needs among Viet Nam civilians everywhere are great but are almost certainly greatest in N.L.F. territory and next in North Viet Nam. Medical and first aid supplies are the priority item and the I.C.R.C. has been shipping these to Hanoi for care of wounded and sick civilians in both North Viet Nam and N.L.F.-controlled territory-those for North Viet Nam being consigned to the Red Cross Society of that country, those for
N.	L.F. territory to an N.L.F. representative in Hanoi whose address was provided-
And again, later:
"The I.C.R.C. urgently needs more money for purchase of supplies as funds donated by the Red Cross Societies of various countries have been largely disbursed. Although permission has not yet been granted for an I.C.R.C. delegate to function in North Viet Nam and N.L.F.-controlled territory, the I.C.R.C. seeks our support of their program in these areas. Acknowledgment of previous shipments to North Viet Nam has been received and Mr. Gallopin has no reason to suspect that the goods have not been properly used. He urges us to participate."
As you will realize, the above represents a change of attitude on our part which resulted from the very useful conversations that I had with Mr. Gallopin of the international committee of the Red Cross in Geneva.
This letter is signed by Major-General A. E. Wrinch, National Commissioner of the Canadian Red Cross Society.
Now I should like to quote from a letter I received from Dr. Inglis dated January 9, in which he says:
The needs of all parts of Viet Nam are recognized by the Canadian Red Cross which has sent assistance to all areas.
The concluding paragraph is as follows:
Meantime, your readers can assist all civilians in Viet Nam by sending donations to this committee at P.O. Box 2543, Vancouver 3, B.C. We have already received more than $20,000 and have set an objective of $50,000 for 1967 because of the escalation of the war. These funds are distributed in the approximate proportions of population and need; 45 per cent to the north, 45 per cent to the National Liberation Front areas, and 10 per cent through the international committee of the Red Cross to civilians in strategic hamlets in Saigon-controlled areas.
That letter is signed by Dr. A. M. Inglis, Chairman of Canadian aid for Viet Nam Civilians, Vancouver.

I am sure the hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Woolliams) would not have asked the question he did had he been fully aware of the facts. This miniscule aid which we Canadians are sending to the people in North Viet Nam and South Viet Nam is a drop in the bucket compared with the millions being spent daily there now, but they serve to indicate to those people that we have a heart for suffering people everywhere. I look forward to hearing the parliamentary secretary's reply.

I
appreciate this opportunity to put on record again the response which was given by the Prime Minister several days ago to the hon. member for Bow River in connection with the question he raised.
As the hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Herridge) has said, some question was raised at that time as to the validity of transfers of funds for medical assistance in North Viet Nam and as to the use to which such funds were being put. I would draw attention to the response given by the Prime Minister on January 26 last as recorded at page 12260 of Hansard in which the right hon. gentleman said:
Our information is that the supplies that may be going to Viet Nam are medical supplies, and there is no authorization required under our law to send medical supplies to any part of the world.
The Prime Minister as well made it clear that there is in no sense a violation of Canadian law in this particular program of sending medical supplies to North Viet Nam.
With respect to the questions and answers on January 24, the hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Herridge) suggested I might be able to clarify the matter further. However, modesty compels me to admit that the answer given by the right hon. gentleman on January 24 as reported at page 12159 cannot be improved upon. After pointing out that there was no objection to transferring funds, or nothing in the law to prevent the transfer of funds, the Prime Minister went on to say:
As to the second aspect of the question, concerning the use made of supplies or funds sent to North Viet Nam once they have reached their destination, we have no knowledge in that regard and I doubt whether the government of North Viet Nam would regard it as within the responsibilities of our representative on the international commission to seek such information.

I understand that the international committee of the Red Cross has endeavoured to obtain this kind of information with respect to its own consignments to North Viet Nam but without avail. The hon. member has also referred to the statement in the letter of Dr. Inglis that no government funds have been made available to North Viet Nam. As was pointed out earlier today by the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Martin), in fact there has been no request for assistance from North Viet Nam.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at the outset I would like to thank the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Laing) for being in the chamber tonight. He is well aware of the subject matter which I wish to raise and his presence shows his concern about it. I am sure that will be appreciated in the community of Fort Smith for which I am now speaking.
I would also like to express my appreciation for the dispatch with which the minister acted in regard to implementing some of the recommendations of the Carrothers commission with respect to the granting of self-government to the Northwest Territories.
Last Monday I asked the minister when he would be able to announce the level and type of assistance from the federal government to be made to the town of Fort Smith, to ensure that no disastrous economic effects could be felt by the Fort Smith community as a result of the movement of many families from Fort Smith to Yellowknife, which has now been declared the capital of the Northwest Territories.
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion
The minister replied to the effect that there was a certain amount of thinking going on in terms of institutional buildings for Fort Smith. I then asked if the minister would consult with his colleague, the Minister of Industry (Mr. Drury), to see if the provisions of the Area Development Incentives Act could be applied to the community and you, Mr. Speaker, suggested that my question was not proper at that time.
Tonight I hope to impress upon the minister that he and his department have responsibility to this town not only in terms of his being the minister responsible for northern development, but in terms of a particular and peculiar responsibility in this special instance. The problem of the community of Fort Smith arose as the result of a decision of the federal government to locate the capital of the Northwest Territories in Yellowknife, as recommended by the Carrothers commission and the Council of the Northwest Territories.
Prior to this decision Fort Smith was considered the administrative centre of the Northwest Territories, and for that matter had been recommended as the capital in 1962 by a previous council, with the result that private industries were counting heavily on the growth of the town in the event that the community was declared the capital. Because the federal government was charged with making the final decision I maintain, as do the residents of Fort Smith, that the federal government has a direct responsibility not only to assist the community but to initiate measures which will ensure stable growth and remove the threat of disaster which now hangs over it like Damocles' sword.
It may be argued that the initiative is up to the territorial government and the townspeople themselves, but I come back to the premise I established a moment ago, that a federal government decision has caused the present chaotic situation, and therefore the federal government, through the minister and his department, has a direct responsibility to bring hope and aid to the town.
There is a precedent for this, Mr. Speaker, in terms of the decision made approximately 12 years ago to abandon the town of Aklavik and create the new town of Inuvik. At that time the federal government subsidized all the business townspeople who wished to move from one town to the other, and I suggest that this might be taken into consideration in the present case.
12724	COMMONS
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion
What is the future of Fort Smith? I am not worried about its future, nor are the townspeople, provided we have the encouragement and incentive of the federal government behind us. We must have now, however, some indication from the federal government about the type and level of assistance which will be available to the town. The town is not standing waiting for the federal government to take the initiative. The mayor of Fort Smith, Mr. Paul Kaiser, will be in Ottawa next Monday, together with the representatives from the town to give the minister his views and ideas concerning how the town can grow and develop. In the meantime there are other ideas. Last week I spent a very delightful two and a half hours with 450 people who are residents of the town. Naturally there was some concern. There was some hostility. However, there was no fright; I think this is extremely important.
It was suggested that this great roads program which has been brought in by the government might be re-evaluated in order that the road development could commence in the area of Fort Smith, rather than at the east arm of Great Slave lake. The Department of Agriculture undertook to do a land survey. I should like to know what the results are.
In the time which remains to me I should like to suggest to the minister that there are two important factors which he must consider. The first concerns the establishment of some type of a prefab housing factory in an area where there is lumber-and that is the Fort Smith area. There is a proposal to build approximately 100 homes in Yellowknife this year. I believe the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development, in consultation with the territorial government and the Department of Industry could bring into effect some form of incentive so that a factory could be established in this particular area to provide the basic prefab facilities for this great growth in Yellowknife itself.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, I should like to impress upon the minister the urgent necessity to establish a university of the north which would include in its curriculum at least the first two years toward a Bachelor of Arts degree. Hopefully the minister will be able to bring together all the interested parties, including members of the territorial government and the federal government, to discuss the matter fully and completely.

There is a herd of buffalo there and we intend to keep them, but they do not need 17,000 square miles. I have spoken to the responsible minister of the province of Alberta and to Premier Manning of Alberta. I told them we would be very happy to negotiate for part of that park to be developed, if we could get compensating land in southern Alberta. I would hope we could carry those negotiations further. There is there an enormous quantity of very high-grade spruce, and the construction of a saw mill, lumber mill and planing mill in Fort Smith is realistic if we could use that timber. This was indicated by my friend the hon. member for Northwest Territories (Mr. Orange).
